newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: INTERVIEW - Avon calling on Asia for growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Avon calling on Asia for growth.

text.p: "Ding-dong, Avon's calling" -- in newly prosperous villages and kampongs throughout Asia and on legions of Asian women working in offices.

The U.S. based cosmetics company, a pioneer in door-to-door direct sales techniques in the United States, is finding its biggest growth markets are in Asia, Avon chairman and chief executive Jim Preston said in an interview on Tuesday.
"Our growth in Asia-Pacific has been 35 percent a year for the past three years," against nine-10 percent annual growth in Europe and the United States, Preston said.

The reason was partly because Avon was starting from a low base in the region, but also because more women were available for door-to-door sales and the region had far fewer retail outlets for cosmetic products outside major cities, he said.

In the 1950s, Avon branded itself on the American consumer with a black-and-white commercial on the new medium of television showing a pert young woman with white gloves ringing a doorbell and telling a housewife: "Avon's calling".

"Ding-dong, Avon's calling is kind of passe," Preston, 64, said. "Because even in the United States, our oldest and most developed market, only about 25 percent of our market is women (sales representatives) knocking on doors."

The company, founded in 1886, had to change with the times. But not before making some "disastrous" acquisitions in the diversification wave of the 1980s and then doing a full make-over of its image, Preston said.
"We went from having no debt and lots of cash in 1982 and by 1988 we had virtually no cash and $1.3 billion in debt."
Preston, who became president and chief executive in 1988 and elected board chairman the following year, sold the non-core business and turned his attention to the marketing side.
"We had a real image issue to overcome," he said. "Our sales reps were hearing 'My mother loves Avon'. We had to go out and completely rebuild our marketing department."
Investors seemed to like the moves. Avon's share price has risen by a multiple of seven times over the past eight years.
Avon's global sales in the year ended last December 31 were $4.8 billion against $4.5 billion in 1995 with a net profit of $317.9 million in 1996 versus $256.5 million the year before.
In the Asia-Pacific market, China was proving to be an especially profitable elixir for the company's bottom line with 120,000 women recruited for door-to-door sales, Preston said.
"By the end of the decade, sales in China will push one-quarter billion dollars," Preston said.
Some 70 percent of Avon's sales were now outside the United States, Preston said.
In line with the trend, Avon is moving towards "global brands", or products and advertising for all markets.
Four years ago, Avon had none. Last year, 26 percent of its sales were from global brands and by 2000 it would be 70 percent, he said.
Global brands meant the company could cut down its inventories by 40 percent and get similar efficiencies and economies of scale in advertising and marketing, he said.
In Malaysia, a new marketing concept for Avon -- setting up Avon boutiques and stalls in small towns and villages -- is raising executive eyebrows.
Avon officials in Malaysia said 126 such stores had been established over the past two years and now accounted for half of all sales in the country.
Preston said the concept might be rolled out elsewhere.
"We're sending our people to Malaysia to find out about what they're doing with these (boutiques)," he said.
"There's more creativity and entrepreneurship in places like Malaysia than in Europe or the United States."
